title: POC scoping: Skyline - latency SLOs & benchmarks
next_steps: Maya to send benchmark template + sample load script (2027-04-16)
Schedule 1-hour benchmark run with Skyline data next Wed (2027-04-21)
Share SOC2 + VPC and KMS docs
action_items: Maya Chen | Send benchmark template, example prompts, and RBAC doc | 2027-04-16
Diego Torres | Prepare Redwood config for TTFT and TPOT tests, include KV cache settings and quantization profile | 2027-04-20
Ben Carter | Deliver representative traffic sample and 2 weeks of traces (anonymized) | 2027-04-15
Aisha Malik | Define success criteria: p95 TTFT <= 350ms for short prompts, p99 TPOT <= 1.2s for 512-token outputs | 2027-04-18
summary: Redwood AE + SE ran a POC scoping with Skyline Retail to define latency/throughput SLOs, workload sizing, benchmark plan, and timeline. Customer wants clear TTFT vs TPOT targets (p95/p99), measurement approach, and a 1-week benchmark run using representative traffic. Agreed next steps: share benchmark template, schedule bench run, and provide Dedicated pilot pricing and security docs.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we got Maya and Diego from Redwood. how's everyone?
[00:08] Aisha (Skyline): Good, thanks. We're excited to run a POC. main thing for us is latency, cost and how this behaves under peak retail traffic.
[00:18] Diego (Redwood SE): Great. to set expectations, today's call we'll scope success criteria, workload sizing, and outline a benchmark plan. we'll cover TTFT vs TPOT definitions and measurement.
[00:28] Ben (Skyline): Quick note: our traffic is spiky (promo windows), about 300 RPS baseline, 1.5k RPS in peaks. typical prompt lengths short for search/autocomplete, sometimes long for personalization requests.
[00:42] Maya: Perfect. maybe we start with definitions—TTFT is time-to-first-token, TPOT is time-to-produce-total or time-to-produce? sorry that's our internal shorthand, Diego?
[00:50] Diego: Yeah — we use TTFT for first token latency, that's useful for UX perceived latency. TPOT we use to mean time-to-last-token or total generation time. in benchmarks we measure both; TTFT matters for chat and streaming, TPOT for full response flows and cost calc. sometimes transcripts show it TTFT vs TTP, so don't worry if it varies in docs.
[01:10] Sofia (Skyline): For us, TTFT target is critical for autocomplete: p95 <= 200-300ms ideally, p99 less than 500ms. For longer outputs used in personalization, we care about p99 TPOT under 1.2s for up to 512 tokens.
[01:28] Diego: That's helpful. can you confirm percent of calls that are short vs long?
[01:31] Ben: Roughly 70% short (<64 tokens), 25% medium (64-256), 5% long (>256). during promos long increases a bit.
[01:40] Maya: Ok so workload mix will guide batching and model selection. ddos — I mean — during peak we need to preserve p95 SLOs, so we might route to dedicated capacity or degrade model size gracefully.
[01:52] Aisha: On security: we'll need VPC, KMS, SOC2 docs. also audit logs for inference.
[01:58] Maya: We'll share SOC2 and VPC architecture docs after the call.
[02:02] Diego: On measurement plan, we recommend two phases: 1) a sandbox functional run with 1–2k synthetic RPS shaped to your trace to validate correctness and tooling; 2) a production-realistic benchmark with your anonymized traffic for 1 hour including a promo spike. We'll capture TTFT/TPOT p50/95/99, CPU/GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate, batching statistics, and token cost.
[02:26] Ben: How do you measure TTFT in streaming? sometimes network overhead skews it.
[02:31] Diego: Good call — we measure at the application edge: time from request accepted by Redwood gateway until first byte of model output hits the client-facing stream. we also instrument server-side timings so we can split network vs model inference. we'll include client-side synthetic checks to capture end-to-end.
[02:47] Raj (Skyline): Will you run tests on our Dedicated pilot or on hosted?
[02:50] Maya: For the POC we can run both. start on hosted to validate config and models, then run on Dedicated nodes configured with your GPU profile to measure steady-state SLOs.
[02:59] Aisha: What about model variants / quantization? we want consistent quality.
[03:03] Diego: We'll test a primary model and a quantized variant. Redwood's runtime supports int8 quantization and different kernel selections; we'll record regression metrics on a small eval prompt set you provide. if quality regression > threshold we won't promote quantized model.
[03:17] Sofia: Can you summarize success criteria again?
[03:19] Maya: Sure. customer-defined: p95 TTFT <= 350ms for short prompts, p99 TPOT <= 1.2s for up-to-512 token responses, <= 5% quality regression on eval set versus baseline. operational: reproducible benchmark run, instrumentation and dashboards, and security compliance docs delivered.
[03:37] Aisha: That works, though we prefer p95 TTFT <= 300ms if feasible.
[03:41] Diego: We'll aim for conservative baseline of 350ms then optimize.
[03:44] [05:00] Speaker 1: (crosstalk).
[05:10] Diego: On workload sizing, based on your numbers: baseline 300 RPS with 1.5k peak. assuming 70% short, effective token throughput is about X, we'll send a sizing spreadsheet.
[05:26] Ben: We can share 14 days of anonymized traces, request IDs removed.
[05:31] Maya: Perfect — please include timestamped latencies too so we can shape promo spikes.
[05:36] Diego: For bench config we'll vary batch sizes, concurrency, and KV cache TTL. caching prefix hits can reduce TTFT significantly for repeated prompts. note: KV cache hit rates are often mis-labeled in quick tests so we'll validate.
[05:52] Aisha: What's your plan for measuring p99? p99 is noisy and needs larger sample windows.
[05:57] Diego: We collect event-level latencies and compute rolling p99 across 1-minute and 5-minute windows; for stability we'll run 1-hour bench with a promo spike to capture tail behavior. we'll also attach trace-level dumps for any tail outliers.
[06:12] Sofia: How long will Redwood need to configure Dedicated for us?
[06:16] Maya: It depends on capacity we allocate — for a small pilot we can provision within 48–72 hours once we have contract details; full-scale Dedicated may take longer.
[06:24] Ben: Pricing estimate?
[06:26] Maya: I'll send pilot pricing and committed capacity options after the call.
[06:30] [10:00] Diego: For instrumentation: we'll provide dashboard templates showing TTFT/TPOT p50/p95/p99, GPU util, token cost per thousand, batching metrics, and KV cache hit %; we'll also hand over the raw CSV/Parquet logs for your team.
[10:18] Raj: Do you support end-to-end tracing with our jaeger?
[10:21] Diego: We integrate with common tracing backends; we can push spans or give an endpoint to pull from Redwood trace logs.
[10:28] Aisha: A few technical clarifications — how do you measure first token when streaming uses chunked encoding?
[10:34] Diego: We detect the first non-empty chunk at the client-facing edge. we also compute server-internal first-token time that excludes network. that helps separate infra network jitter from model time.
[10:44] Ben: For the KV cache, do you support cross-request caching or only within a session?
[10:48] Diego: Redwood supports prefix/KV caching across sessions for identical prompts if configured; TTLs and privacy constraints are configurable. we'll include a recommended cache policy for your workload.
[11:00] Maya: Ok, timeline proposal: today share templates; by 2027-04-15 Skyline sends traces and eval prompts; Redwood prepares bench config by 2027-04-20; run bench 2027-04-21; analysis and dashboard review 2027-04-22/23.
[11:18] Aisha: That timeline looks reasonable.
[11:21] Diego: On TTFT vs TPOT tradeoffs — sometimes reducing TTFT requires smaller model or more memory to avoid long scheduling delays. we can also enable streaming so first token comes sooner even if TPOT stays similar.
[11:36] Sofia: If we accept slightly higher TPOT for long responses but keep TTFT low for UX, that's acceptable.
[11:41] Diego: Good note — that's a typical operational tradeoff, and we can set route policies that prefer lower-latency variants for interactive endpoints.
[11:51] Ben: Do you capture token-level cost metrics?
[11:54] Maya: Yes, our dashboards include cost per 1k tokens and estimated monthly run-rate based on the traffic sample you provide.
[12:02] [20:00] Speaker 2: (brief hold music)
[20:30] Diego: A few gotchas to call out: warmup behavior matters. if you run sudden spikes without warmup, p99 will spike; we'll capture warmup curves and recommend pre-warm policies. also padding and tokenization differences across models can shift TPOT; we'll normalize via same tokenization pipeline.
[20:56] Aisha: We also need SLOs for error rates and fallback behavior — if a heavy spike causes latency to exceed SLO, we need graceful degradation (e.g., fall back to cached result or smaller model).
[21:07] Maya: We'll include fallback policies in the plan — canary, automatic fallback to smaller variant, circuit breaking.
[21:15] Diego: For the bench we'll also run a degradation scenario: route 20% of traffic to a fallback variant and measure impact.
[21:24] Ben: On data residency — some EU traffic needs to stay in region. can you route by region?
[21:29] Maya: Yes, routing by region is supported; we'll document the region mapping for the POC.
[21:35] Sofia: If we hit a quality regression with quantized models, will Redwood help tune quantization?
[21:40] Diego: Yes, we'll try different quantization profiles and kernel choices; if needed we'll recommend alternate models.
[21:46] Aisha: For p99 measurement windows — do you use global p99 or per-minute sliding window?
[21:50] Diego: Both. we compute global p99 for the run and per-minute sliding p99 to surface transient spikes. the per-minute helps catch short promo-induced tails.
[21:58] Maya: Any other blockers from Skyline side?
[22:01] Ben: We'll need access controls for Redwood engineers to the test env — temporary SSO accounts and scoped roles.
[22:07] Maya: Okay we'll propose RBAC roles: bench-admin, bench-reader, and revoke after POC.
[22:12] Aisha: Good. can we get a short checklist for the data we need to share?
[22:16] Maya: Sure — we'll include: 14 days anonymized traces, sample prompts and expected outputs for eval set, tokenization examples, and traffic shaping instructions.
[22:25] Diego: Also include any latency goals by endpoint — you might have different targets for search vs personalization.
[22:32] Sofia: We do. search is stricter.
[22:35] Maya: Final recap: agreed SLOs draft: p95 TTFT <= 350ms target (aim for 300ms), p99 TPOT <= 1.2s for up-to-512 tokens, rollouts include quantized variant only if quality regression <5%. Redwood to share templates, schedule bench, and provide pricing + SOC2/VPC docs.
[22:58] Aisha: Thanks, that covers it.
[23:02] Ben: Thanks everyone.
[23:05] Maya: I'll follow up with the benchmark package and next steps notes.
[23:10] Diego: We'll also attach a short runbook for measuring TTFT/TPOT and how to interpret p99 noise.
[23:16] Sofia: Great.
[23:18] [57:00] End of recording.

Notes: transcript contains occasional mis-hearings (time-to-produce sometimes transcribed as time-to-produce-total or TTP), speaker labels occasionally generic, and filler words retained to preserve natural speech.
